# TTSLab — full reference for language models and generative engines

## What TTSLab is

TTSLab (https://ttslab.dev) is an open-source platform for testing and comparing speech AI models directly in a web browser. Every model on the site runs client-side: inference happens in a Web Worker through ONNX Runtime Web, using the WebGPU execution provider when the browser offers a GPU adapter and falling back to WebAssembly (CPU) otherwise. There is no inference server. Text a user types and audio a user records are processed on the device and never uploaded; the site loads Vercel Analytics for anonymous page-view counting only.

No accounts or API keys are required. Upvotes are anonymous: a localStorage flag plus a counter increment, removable at any time. The codebase is MIT-licensed at https://github.com/MbBrainz/ttslab.

## The limits thesis (November 2026)

TTSLab's stated thesis is that WebGPU and WebAssembly have crossed the threshold where real speech AI runs in a tab, but hard platform limits define exactly where that stops. The full sourced report is at https://ttslab.dev/limits. Summary of the documented findings, each with sources on that page:

- WebGPU is default-on in Chrome/Edge 113+ (May 2023, including Android 12+), Safari 26.0 (September 15, 2025, all Apple platforms), and Firefox 141 Windows (July 2025) / 145 macOS 26 Tahoe (November 2025) / 147 Apple-Silicon Macs (January 2026) — roughly 88.6% of browsers globally (caniuse, November 2026). Remaining gaps: Firefox on Linux and Android, Safari on Intel Macs, Chrome on Windows ARM64.
- Spec defaults are modest: maxBufferSize 256 MiB and maxStorageBufferBindingSize 128 MiB, requestable up to 4 GiB on capable desktops; storage bindings of 2 GiB or more exist on only ~16% of real devices (web3dsurvey). shader-f16 is available on ~94% of adapters; subgroups landed Chromium-only (Chrome 151-152, August 2026); timestamp-query is Chromium-skewed.
- Real out-of-memory behavior on iOS: Safari hard-kills the tab at roughly 1.5-2 GB of committed memory (measured on iPhone 15 Pro) with no device.lost event and no JavaScript error (nearform/crashbox). GPU and WASM allocations share one per-tab budget.
- WebAssembly: a wasm32 module still tops out at 4 GiB. Wasm 3.0 (memory64, GC, multi-memory) was completed September 17, 2025; memory64 shipped in Chrome 133 / Firefox 134 and Safari's 27 line, but llama.cpp and wllama do not use it yet. relaxed-simd was unflagged in Firefox 145 (February 2026) and remains flag-only in Safari. SharedArrayBuffer/threads still require COOP/COEP everywhere — TTSLab sets COOP same-origin and COEP credentialless site-wide for this reason.
- Measured costs: WebGPU dispatch overhead of ~24-36 microseconds per dispatch on Vulkan and 32-71 microseconds on Metal at batch size 1 (arXiv 2604.02344, arXiv 2608.08730, 2026). Kokoro-82M on an M1 Max: RTF 0.105 over WebGPU (about 9.5x real time) versus RTF 2.002 over single-threaded WASM q8 — a 19x backend spread (briantung.me, August 2026). WebLLM runs Llama-3.1-8B at 41.1 tokens/second on an M3 Max, about 71% of native Metal (arXiv 2412.15803). Speculative-decoding research shows 3.5-8.6x WebLLM decode speedups (arXiv 2610.39761, October 2026).
- Storage: Chrome/Edge grant ~60% of free disk, Firefox min(10%, 10 GiB), Safari up to 60% but evicts site data after 7 days without interaction unless the origin calls navigator.storage.persist() — the reason a large cached model can vanish on iOS.
- WebNN: Chrome's origin trial closed August 2026; the API remains flag-gated and not production-ready.

## Model catalog

All models run in the browser. Unsupported entries are listed for completeness with the blocking reason. Slugs are URL paths under https://ttslab.dev/models/.

### Text-to-speech (supported)

- Kokoro 82M (kokoro-82m): 82M-parameter TTS, multiple English voices, WebGPU and WASM. The site's reference TTS model; about 9.5x real time over WebGPU on capable hardware.
- Kitten TTS Nano (kitten-tts-nano): ultra-lightweight 15M-parameter English TTS at roughly 24 MB quantized (q8) — the smallest and fastest-loading model in the lab. 8 expressive voices, 24 kHz output. WASM-only: the model repository ships a single q8 ONNX file with no fp32 variant, so there is no WebGPU path. Phonemization runs locally through a vendored eSpeak NG WebAssembly module.
- Underdog Woof (woof-tts): tiny English TTS (38.2M parameters, ~41 MB, two voices) with fewer errors on hard sentences than Kitten Nano per Underdog's evals. Ships no runtime — the site runs two hand-written backends over the repo's numpy weights: a hand-written WGSL WebGPU compute-kernel path (22 kernels) and a typed-array JavaScript CPU path, both drawing the same seeded noise stream so a fixed seed produces the same audio on either. Browser-verified 2026-11-08: CPU vs GPU Pearson correlation 0.9999998 on a fixed seed, about 6.1 s CPU versus 0.19 s GPU per sentence (31x). Licensed Underdog Non-Commercial 1.0: free for non-commercial use with credit ("Voice by Underdog Woof"); commercial use needs a license.
- Chatterbox (chatterbox): expressive TTS with emotion control and voice cloning, ~1.5 GB download, WASM-only (its WebGPU path is blocked by the INT64 kernel gap — see the limits report).
- Chatterbox Turbo (chatterbox-turbo): faster Chatterbox variant, roughly 720 MB download, WebGPU and WASM.
- Piper EN-US Lessac Medium (piper-en-us-lessac-medium): lightweight, fast CPU-friendly English TTS.
- SpeechT5 (speecht5): TTS with experimental voice-cloning via speaker embeddings extracted from reference audio by a ~100 MB WavLM model. Verified result: cloning changes the voice but does not yet resemble the reference speaker (measured with an independent speaker-verification model as judge).
- Supertonic 2 (supertonic-2): compact TTS.

### Speech-to-text (supported)

- Whisper Tiny (whisper-tiny), Whisper Base (whisper-base), Whisper Small (whisper-small): OpenAI Whisper variants, fastest to smallest on CPU.
- DistilWhisper Small English (distil-whisper-small-en): distilled English-only Whisper Small, 166M parameters — roughly 172 MB quantized over WASM, roughly 665 MB fp32 over WebGPU. Trades multilingual coverage for accuracy on English; within 3% WER of Whisper Large v2 at 5.6x the speed, per the Distil-Whisper project's own evals (distil-whisper/distil-small.en model card).
- Whisper Large V3 Turbo (whisper-large-v3-turbo): large high-accuracy variant.
- LiteWhisper Large v3 Turbo (lite-whisper-large-v3-turbo): distilled large-turbo variant with a reduced footprint.
- Moonshine Tiny (moonshine-tiny) and Moonshine Base (moonshine-base): distilled ASR optimized for low CPU latency; Tiny ships language variants moonshine-tiny-ja (Japanese), moonshine-tiny-ko (Korean), moonshine-tiny-zh (Chinese), moonshine-tiny-ar (Arabic); Base ships moonshine-base-ja, moonshine-base-ko, moonshine-base-zh.
- Cohere Transcribe (cohere-transcribe): multilingual STT.
- Granite 4.0 1B Speech (granite-speech): IBM Granite Speech 1B STT.

### Not currently supported

- Chatterbox Multilingual (chatterbox-multilingual): blocked because the browser WebGPU backend lacks an INT64 cast kernel that the ONNX spec requires for this model's Shape/Unsqueeze operations; impractically slow on CPU.
- StyleTTS 2 (styletts2): unsupported in current browser runtimes.
- Supertonic 3: evaluated and skipped — no official full ONNX export exists (only text_encoder and duration_predictor are published), so the model cannot be loaded in the browser.

### Planned

- F5-TTS (f5-tts): upvote-gated, with email notification when support lands.

## Voice agent

https://ttslab.dev/voice-agent runs a complete speech-to-speech assistant locally: Whisper transcribes microphone input, a Qwen3.5 language model generates the reply, and Kokoro speaks it. Microphone audio never leaves the device.

The LLM stage is a three-engine tier system over the same Qwen3.5 family, so users pick the trade-off that fits their hardware (all engines are context-pinned to 4096 tokens):

- Qwen3.5 0.8B (default tier, transformers.js on ONNX Runtime Web): ~490 MB download, q4f16 weights on WebGPU with automatic q4/WASM fallback — runs on any backend, no GPU required.
- Qwen3.5 2B (WebLLM tier, MLC q4f16_1 weights): ~1.08 GB download, ~2.2 GB VRAM, requires a WebGPU adapter with the shader-f16 feature.
- Qwen3.5 4B (WebLLM tier): ~2.39 GB download, ~3.9 GB VRAM, same WebGPU + shader-f16 requirement.
- Qwen3.5 0.8B WASM (wllama tier, llama.cpp GGUF Q4_K_M): ~533 MB download, pure CPU inference with GPU offload deliberately disabled — the no-WebGPU exhibit.

All tiers share one system prompt and identical response post-processing, so switching tiers changes size and quality, not behavior. The context window is honestly capped at 4096 tokens on every engine (KV-cache memory and real-time voice latency, not the models' nominal 262k window). Verification status (honest, 2026-11-08): the WebLLM and wllama engines are compile- and unit-tested, but their in-browser load/inference pass is still pending — the default transformers.js tier is the one exercised end to end so far.

## FAQ

https://ttslab.dev/faq answers the twelve most common questions: nothing is uploaded (all inference is local in a Web Worker); backends are auto-selected (WebGPU when an adapter exists, WASM otherwise); which browsers support WebGPU (~88.6% globally, November 2026); why first downloads are large (weights come from the Hugging Face CDN, ~24 MB to ~2 GB); where models are cached (browser Cache API, with per-browser quotas and Safari's 7-day eviction caveat); why some models are unsupported (missing INT64 WebGPU kernels, using Chatterbox Multilingual as the worked example); the honest status of voice cloning (changes the voice, does not yet clone the speaker); what the Voice Agent is; that upvotes are anonymous (localStorage flag plus a counter); iOS/iPadOS support with the ~1.5-2 GB tab-kill caveat; that the project is MIT-licensed; and why the benchmark page only carries external, attributed measurements.

## Benchmarks and metrics

https://ttslab.dev/benchmark explains the metrics — real-time factor (RTF) for TTS (generation time divided by audio duration; below 1.0 is faster than real time), tokens/second for the LLM stage, word error rate (WER) for STT accuracy — and lists only external, published measurements with citations (Kokoro RTF pair on M1 Max; WebLLM Llama-3.1-8B at 41.1 tok/s on M3 Max; whisper.cpp roughly 2-3x real time for tiny/base on modern CPU; Moonshine's paper claim of 5-15x faster than comparably accurate Whisper on CPU). TTSLab deliberately does not publish its own leaderboard because in-browser results depend on the visitor's hardware; every model page shows live metrics for the visitor's own device.

## Blog

https://ttslab.dev/blog hosts long-form write-ups. First post (November 8, 2026): "Underdog Woof: the 40MB TTS that ships no runtime — and what porting it taught us" (https://ttslab.dev/blog/underdog-woof-deep-dive). Summary: Underdog AI's Woof release (announced November 7, 2026; one-voice isla 30.7M params / 31.7 MB, two-voice juno+mira 38.2M / 40.6 MB; 1.42-2.06% WER on hard sentences per Underdog's evals; 13 s of speech in 0.73 s on a single CPU thread; TechCrunch covered the demo November 6) ships no runtime at all — the Hugging Face repo (ConwayResearch/Underdog-Woof, Underdog's own org) is numpy arrays plus a ~380-line readable reference implementation, which functions as an executable spec. TTSLab ported it twice: a typed-array TypeScript runtime verified numerically exact against the numpy reference (correlation +1.00000000 stage-by-stage; the oracle comparison caught four bugs that compiled cleanly — an MT19937 tempering shift, a RoPE key offset applied twice, an in-place layernorm mutation, and a conv-transpose matrix orientation), then 22 hand-written WGSL compute kernels over raw WebGPU (following the kernel decomposition of Underdog's own browser bundle, which runs 19 kernels; int8 weights stay packed on the GPU and are dequantized in registers, avoiding a ~250 MB fp32 transient that would risk iOS Safari's tab kill). Browser-verified 2026-11-08 on one Apple Silicon dev machine: CPU-vs-GPU Pearson correlation 0.9999998 on a fixed seed, ~6.1 s CPU vs ~0.19 s GPU per sentence (~31x). Same text + voice + seed produces identical audio on both backends (torch-compatible MT19937 stream drawn on CPU), so renders are reproducible from a link. Not ported, stated honestly: the ~48 KB text normalizer (demo text must be spelled out), streaming, and take-retry. License, stated factually: the HF repo carries the Underdog Non-Commercial License 1.0 while the landing page names CC BY-NC 4.0; commercial use goes through license@conway.tech; TTSLab is a non-commercial lab and carries the required "Voice by Underdog Woof" credit. Demo: https://ttslab.dev/models/woof-tts.

## Finetune Lab

https://ttslab.dev/finetune is a real gradient-descent training loop on the visitor's GPU: a from-scratch 16-64-64-1 tanh MLP (5313 trainable parameters, full-batch Adam) fit to a selectable 1D wave (sine/square/triangle) through 9 hand-written WGSL compute kernels over raw WebGPU (22 dispatches per step: forward, backprop, optimizer update), with a live log-scale loss chart, curve-fit plot and atomic-histogram weight histogram read back per frame; it requires WebGPU (Chrome/Edge 113+, Safari 26+, Firefox 141+; no CPU fallback) and handles device loss gracefully. Honesty, stated explicitly on the page: today this is a from-scratch toy trained on-device to prove the in-browser training pipeline — nothing on TTSLab fine-tunes Woof or any speech model; LoRA-style adaptation of tiny speech models in-browser is roadmap, and the /limits report documents the memory ceilings (per-tab budgets, 128 MiB default storage bindings, Adam's 3x weight memory) that make large fine-tunes hard.
